extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, patent practitioners, and scholars studying patent law (specification/claim construction and trial procedure)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules for construing patent specifications, assessing sufficiency/practicability, determining patentable subject matter and infringement, and the respective roles of court and jury. Focused on how evidence, words of art, and surrounding circumstances affect legal construction and factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction may rest on facts referred to as part of the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, the construction may rest on facts, which are so referred to as to make a part of the description and to govern it. If these facts are controverted, they are to be left to the jury. But if they are proved, or admitted, the court will take notice of them in giving a legal construction to the instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: specification describing an improvement and referring to admitted facts (Davoll v. Brown / bow-flyer). If factual statements are incorporated into the description they can govern claim construction; if disputed they go to the jury, if proved the court will consider them in construing the instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee is to be understood as claiming things 'in use', not every theoretical possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must be understood to mean things that were in use, and not every thing which would produce [an effect] but, from being so expensive, was never expected to be in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: gas-from-oil—although oil would yield gas as a philosophical fact, the apparatus described could not be used advantageously for oil at the time; court construes claims to refer to practical things in use rather than merely theoretic possibilities or economically impracticable materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must describe invention with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee should describe, with reasonable certainty, his invention; the Act of Congress requires that he 'shall, particularly, specify and point the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: enable the public to know whether they violate the patent and, after expiry, to make the machines correctly; this statutory requirement informs both claim drafting and judicial scrutiny of sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give liberal construction to patents when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal construction is to be given to a patent, and inventors sustained, if practicable, without a departure from sound principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rationale: encourage ingenuity and perseverance; courts should sustain patents if they can fairly be read to cover the invention, but only consistent with sound legal principles and statutory requirements (see jury instructions to consider liberal views unless specification is so clear others could readily make machines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of description to enable competent persons is a question of fact for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of the description, to enable competent persons to apply the invention, is a question of fact for the jury, on the testimony of experts and the language itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: court tells the jury what the specification says; jury then decides whether the directions are sufficiently clear and explicit to enable a competent workman to practice the invention. Expert testimony and the plain language both bear on this factual determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court declares what the specification has said; jury decides practicability/intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The information of what the specification has said, is to come from the court; although it may happen that in determining the meaning the aid of the jury will be required to ascertain the meaning of words of art or the surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When words of art or surrounding circumstances affect meaning, the court instructs the jury that the specification 'has said so and so' according to their findings. If there are no words of art or surrounding circumstances to be ascertained, the court alone construes the specification; the jury then assesses whether the described directions enable practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence may affect construction but cannot be used to supply positive omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff is always entitled to say that his specification requires the explanation of facts to determine the extent of his claim and the character of his invention; the court is to receive and watch the evidence, and to apply it to the construction, taking care that it be not allowed to go so far as to supply positive omissions, which would render the specification defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit: evidence can be used to explain terms of art or surrounding circumstances and thus affect claim meaning, but it must not be permitted to fill in essential omissions in the written specification that the statute requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate the court's legal construction role from the jury's factual role
rubrics_metrics.description: The provinces of the court and the jury are distinct: the court determines the meaning of the specification (legal construction) after facts bearing on that meaning are ascertained; the jury determines factual questions such as whether the specification's directions are sufficient to enable practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical cautions: avoid letting the jury 'decide what the claim is' when they are tasked with intelligibility/practicability. Courts should separate the legal question of what the paper means from the factual question of whether it enables practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether directions are calculated to mislead a workman is for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal question whether the directions were calculated to mislead a workman (by stating that which was not true) is a question for the jury, but before it can be determined it is necessary to ascertain what the specification has said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson v. Harford example: the disputed meaning of 'effect' required the court to construe the term before the jury could decide whether the specification's statement was misleading; the jury resolves the factual question of misleadingness based on that construction and the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of specification is for the court but may be conditional on facts
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases the meaning of the specification is for the court; this must be done either by taking into view at the time the evidence which bears upon the meaning (where not controverted), or by leaving to the jury matters of fact to ascertain the meaning of scientific words or surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence bearing on meaning is undisputed the court may give an absolute construction; when meaning depends on disputed facts the court gives a conditional construction and leaves the factual issues to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether invention is a proper subject for a patent is a question of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the invention disclosed by the specification is a proper subject for a patent is a question of law, on which the court will instruct the jury; it may involve the finding of a variety of facts but, when ascertained, it is purely a question of law whether the invention is a patentable subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from novelty: patentable subject-matter (legal classification, e.g., mere new use vs patentable invention) is decided by the court after facts are found; novelty (is it new?) remains a factual matter for the jury or factfinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is a prerequisite and is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of the invention is a pre-requisite to the validity of the patent, and this is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty via evidence of prior art and public use; even if novel, court must still decide whether it falls within classes the patent laws protect (legal question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement is a factual determination of substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of infringement is whether the invention of the defendant is substantially the same thing as that of the plaintiff. The identity of two things is a matter of fact, depending upon evidence; it is for the jury to determine, under proper instructions, whether the two things are the same or different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial procedure: jury decides infringement as a factual inquiry under judicial guidance on claim scope and principles of identity/diversity in patent law (see cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should sustain specifications if they can be fairly construed
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must be sustained if they can be fairly; courts should not be astute to avoid inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive stance: read specifications practically rather than on 'mere metaphysical distinctions'; where a fair construction supports validity and intelligibility courts should uphold the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to grant patents and judicial approach to retroactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has general power to promote progress by securing exclusive rights to inventors and may pass laws (even retrospectively) granting or confirming patents; but statutes ought not to be construed to operate retrospectively unless such a construction is unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional/legal guidance: courts lean to benign constructions avoiding retroactive liability; example discussion of Acts granting renewed or retrospective patents (Blanchard/Blanchard v. Sprague, Evans v. Eaton). This affects remedial and jurisdictional questions surrounding patents.
